Lumentum’s optoelectronic parts sold out through 2029 as AI demand outruns supply
The laser and optical component maker says hyperscaler demand has pushed its sell-out window out by roughly a year in just six months
Lumentum has a problem most companies would trade their entire marketing budget for. Its optoelectronic components are fully spoken for through 2029, according to Bloomberg, as tech companies race to build AI data centers.
The update came on October 9, 2026. Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ: LITE) said its capacity for these parts is sold out through nearly 2029.
The products in question are mostly advanced indium phosphide (InP) devices, including EML chips and pump lasers. These are light-based components. They help move data at the speeds AI infrastructure now demands.
The details: demand keeps outrunning the factory
Most of the buying pressure is coming from hyperscalers and other tech firms. Their goal is ultra-fast data centers built for AI workloads, and those facilities need a lot of optical hardware.
CEO Michael Hurlston acknowledged that Lumentum is still struggling to keep up with customers, despite significant work to expand production.
The size of that gap is striking. For certain products, unmet demand is projected at approximately 70% in 2027 and roughly 30% into 2028.

The timeline is the other headline. In April 2026, Lumentum expected to be fully sold out through 2028. By October, that window had stretched to nearly 2029.
Background: the numbers behind the backlog
In fiscal Q4 2026, which ended in June 2026, Lumentum reported revenue of $1.01 billion. That figure was up 109% year over year. The company credited most of that growth to its components segment, the same business now facing the capacity crunch.
Then there is Nvidia. In March 2026, the chip giant invested $2 billion in Lumentum. That money was tied to multibillion-dollar purchase commitments for Lumentum’s lasers and optical components.
What this means for AI infrastructure and investors
The downside sits with everyone downstream. Companies that rely on Lumentum’s parts may run into shortages. A 70% shortfall on certain products in 2027 is not a rounding error for those buyers. It could force tough choices about which projects get built first and which ones wait.
For anyone tracking the AI buildout, a few signals are worth watching. One is whether Lumentum’s capacity additions start narrowing the unmet demand figures for 2027 and 2028. Another is whether the sold-out window keeps sliding further out. It moved from 2028 to nearly 2029 between April and October. A third is how Lumentum’s components revenue tracks in coming quarters. The 109% jump in fiscal Q4 2026 set a high bar. Sustaining growth will depend less on finding buyers and more on how fast the company can turn new production capacity into finished parts.

Lumentum (LITE) Can’t Meet Demand. Can Its Valuation Hold Up?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 8:33 AM CDT 3 min read
According to Lumentum Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:LITE) CEO Michael Hurlston, the company is now almost sold out of components for 2029, as he said in a recent interview. Just six months ago, he said Lumentum was on track to sell out by 2028. The demand outlook is strong, but Lumentum's strong demand raises the question of how much growth is already priced in. Meanwhile, see our Top 10 Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) Stocks to Buy in 2026 to see the 5 companies that rank higher than LITE.
Lumentum Can’t Meet 70% of Demand for Some Products. Why That’s Bullish and Risky for the Stock
The underlying details paint a more limited picture. Lumentum cannot meet about 70% of demand for certain products through next year. For some other products, supply constraints will leave 30% of demand unmet through 2028.
According to Wedbush Securities' Matt Bryson, this creates a favorable backdrop for optical-input suppliers such as AXT and for foundry and silicon photonics companies, including Tower Semiconductor and GlobalFoundries. The challenge is not a lack of demand but limited capacity. LITE's growth will depend on how quickly it can expand production. Lumentum's challenge is turning strong demand into actual sales, but which other aggressive growth stocks do Wall Street analysts see as having room to run?
Is a 46x Multiple Fair?
Lumentum's forward P/E stands at 45.70x, roughly 22% above its five-year average of 37.51x. This indicates that investors are paying more than they have historically. That premium reflects expectations for rapid earnings growth. EPS is projected to grow 151.24% this fiscal year from a small base, followed by another 64.80% increase next year. Based on current estimates, the P/E could decline to roughly 28x on 2028 earnings and 21x on 2029 earnings. This means much of the earnings investors are paying for today is expected to arrive within one to three years. The company's near sold-out capacity lends more support to those projections.
The stock is not undervalued, but its premium could be reasonable if Lumentum adds capacity as planned. Demand is already there; production capacity is now the key factor limiting growth.
According to our database, the number of hedge funds holding Lumentum fell from 123 at the end of Q1 2026 to 111 at the end of Q2 2026. Short interest reached 8.96% of float as of September 30, 2026.
While demand remains firm and Wedbush sees potential benefits for Lumentum's suppliers, investor positioning tells a more cautious story. The decline in hedge fund ownership and short interest approaching 9% suggest that some investors remain skeptical of the premium valuation. Whether Lumentum can build capacity quickly enough will determine if its premium valuation can hold.
While we acknowledge the potential of LITE as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Optics Names Advance on Earnings Anticipation

Similarities among Applied Optoelectronics, Lumentum, and Coherent include exposure to AI networking demand and optical components for data centers. The broader chip sector has also shown signs of stabilizing after a recent soft stretch.
Upcoming earnings will provide the next major checkpoints for order visibility and margin trends across the three companies. Lumentum’s multiyear capacity constraints and Coherent’s PhotonLink ramp offer potential catalysts if demand remains robust. Applied Optoelectronics faces similar questions around AI optical adoption and competitive positioning.

As artificial intelligence (AI) pushes computing power and data transmission to new limits, investors are weighing different paths to growth. Is Arm Holdings (ARM -3.06%) or Lumentum Holdings (LITE -1.44%) the better choice today?
Arm creates the foundational blueprints for the world's most energy-efficient processors. Lumentum provides the optical components that allow data centers to communicate at lightning speeds. Both companies are central to the infrastructure of modern computing, but they operate with vastly different business models and financial profiles.
Arm designs and licenses central processing units (CPUs) and other systems used in everything from smartphones to high-performance data centers. Rather than manufacturing chips, the company earns revenue through licensing fees and royalties on every chip sold. This model enables high scalability and profit margins in the semiconductor industry.
In fiscal 2026 (ending in March), Arm's revenue reached $4.9 billion. This represents growth of nearly 23% compared to the prior year. Net income was roughly $698 million, though the net margin decreased slightly from roughly 16% in the previous year to about 14%.
As of its June 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1x, indicating the company has very little debt relative to its net equity. The current ratio is roughly 5.3x, suggesting a strong ability to meet short-term financial obligations.
Trailing-12-month (TTM) free cash flow was $1.5 billion through the June quarter, but note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 69% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Lumentum manufactures optical and photonic products essential to cloud data centers and telecommunications networks. In its latest fiscal year ended June 27, 2026, Lumentum revealed that Customer A accounted for approximately 26.6% of revenue while Customer B accounted for roughly 15%. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as the loss of either client would be significant.
For fiscal 2026, the company reported revenue of $3 billion, which was an increase of about 83% over the prior year. Despite this massive top-line growth, the company reported a net loss of approximately $6.9 billion, although its operating profit (earnings before interest and taxes) was $525 million. The $6.9 billion net loss was due to a $7.7 billion non-recurring loss on debt extinguishment.
According to its June 2026 balance sheet, the company has a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.4x. The current ratio is nearly 1.7x, indicating about $1.70 in short-term assets for every $1.00 of short-term debt.
TTM free cash flow for the period was roughly $300 million. However, stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 22.7% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Arm faces intense competition from established rivals and open-source alternatives. If major tech companies decide to design their own architectures rather than paying licensing fees, the company could see its market share erode. Additionally, the business relies on continued growth in the mobile and data center markets, and any slowdown in hardware upgrades would impact its royalty income.
Lumentum is highly dependent on a small number of customers for a significant portion of its sales, and many relationships lack long-term volume commitments. The company is also subject to complex trade policies and export controls, specifically regarding operations in China. Competition from global firms such as IPG Photonics and Viavi Solutions exerts constant pressure on pricing and operating margins.
Lumentum appears to be the more value-oriented choice as it trades at a significant discount to its peer across both sales and future earnings estimates.
Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Arm is a great business that generates high margins from royalties and licensing fees. It would be a solid chip stock to own, but Lumentum offers better value right now.
Analysts expect Arm to grow earnings at a 25% annualized rate in the coming years. However, Lumentum is expected to deliver 132% annualized growth, as the business scales and expands margins. Relative to their forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios, Arm looks expensive, trading at a forward P/E-to-growth (PEG) ratio of 4.3x, while Lumentum trades at an attractive 0.29x.
Lumentum is benefiting from data centers shifting to optical connectivity for AI workloads. Revenue surged 109% year over year in the recent quarter, marking the eighth consecutive quarter of growth and signaling strong momentum that may not be fully reflected in the stock's valuation right now.
Arm is benefiting from the growing demand for CPUs, and its expertise in designing power-efficient chips could help it gain market share in the data center market.
Both companies are meeting demand at crucial chokepoints for AI, and they both face comparable risks. But it's difficult for me to pass up the huge discrepancy between each stock's PEG ratios. I would buy Lumentum since it's growing much faster than Arm and commands a much lower premium for future earnings growth.

As artificial intelligence (AI) pushes computing power and data transmission to new limits, investors are weighing different paths to growth. Is Arm Holdings (ARM -3.06%) or Lumentum Holdings (LITE -1.44%) the better choice today?
Arm creates the foundational blueprints for the world's most energy-efficient processors. Lumentum provides the optical components that allow data centers to communicate at lightning speeds. Both companies are central to the infrastructure of modern computing, but they operate with vastly different business models and financial profiles.
Arm designs and licenses central processing units (CPUs) and other systems used in everything from smartphones to high-performance data centers. Rather than manufacturing chips, the company earns revenue through licensing fees and royalties on every chip sold. This model enables high scalability and profit margins in the semiconductor industry.
In fiscal 2026 (ending in March), Arm's revenue reached $4.9 billion. This represents growth of nearly 23% compared to the prior year. Net income was roughly $698 million, though the net margin decreased slightly from roughly 16% in the previous year to about 14%.
As of its June 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1x, indicating the company has very little debt relative to its net equity. The current ratio is roughly 5.3x, suggesting a strong ability to meet short-term financial obligations.
Trailing-12-month (TTM) free cash flow was $1.5 billion through the June quarter, but note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 69% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Lumentum manufactures optical and photonic products essential to cloud data centers and telecommunications networks. In its latest fiscal year ended June 27, 2026, Lumentum revealed that Customer A accounted for approximately 26.6% of revenue while Customer B accounted for roughly 15%. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as the loss of either client would be significant.
For fiscal 2026, the company reported revenue of $3 billion, which was an increase of about 83% over the prior year. Despite this massive top-line growth, the company reported a net loss of approximately $6.9 billion, although its operating profit (earnings before interest and taxes) was $525 million. The $6.9 billion net loss was due to a $7.7 billion non-recurring loss on debt extinguishment.
According to its June 2026 balance sheet, the company has a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.4x. The current ratio is nearly 1.7x, indicating about $1.70 in short-term assets for every $1.00 of short-term debt.
TTM free cash flow for the period was roughly $300 million. However, stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 22.7% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Arm faces intense competition from established rivals and open-source alternatives. If major tech companies decide to design their own architectures rather than paying licensing fees, the company could see its market share erode. Additionally, the business relies on continued growth in the mobile and data center markets, and any slowdown in hardware upgrades would impact its royalty income.
Lumentum is highly dependent on a small number of customers for a significant portion of its sales, and many relationships lack long-term volume commitments. The company is also subject to complex trade policies and export controls, specifically regarding operations in China. Competition from global firms such as IPG Photonics and Viavi Solutions exerts constant pressure on pricing and operating margins.

Arm is a great business that generates high margins from royalties and licensing fees. It would be a solid chip stock to own, but Lumentum offers better value right now.

Arm is benefiting from the growing demand for CPUs, and its expertise in designing power-efficient chips could help it gain market share in the data center market.

LUMENTUM ANNOUNCES FOURTH QUARTER AND FULL FISCAL YEAR 2026 RESULTS
Fiscal Fourth Quarter Highlights:
•GAAP gross margin of 47.4%; Non-GAAP gross margin of 50.4%
•GAAP operating margin of 27.8%; Non-GAAP operating margin of 36.6%
•Forecasting first quarter of fiscal year 2027 revenue of $1.225 billion to $1.275 billion; Non-GAAP operating margin of 39.5% to 40.5%; and Non-GAAP diluted net income per share of $4.05 to $4.35
San Jose, Calif., August 11, 2026 – Lumentum Holdings Inc. (“Lumentum” or the “Company”) today reported results for its fiscal fourth quarter and full fiscal year ended June 27, 2026.
“Lumentum is positioned at the heart of a secular industry shift. As AI compute workloads increase in both speed and bandwidth, data center architects are turning to optical links as a primary means of connectivity. While our Q4 results demonstrate broad-based traction, key growth drivers such as OCS solutions and our cloud module business, where we are advancing 1.6T adoption, are beginning to layer in. Increasing demand for ultra-high-power CPO lasers, an initial order for ELS modules, as well as our breadth of NPO engagements are the first signs that optics are starting to penetrate in-rack connectivity, significantly upping our optical TAM,” said President and CEO Michael Hurlston.
“Looking ahead, our trajectory continues to accelerate as AI demand drives our Q1 revenue guidance midpoint to $1.25 billion, reaching our target model more than a quarter ahead of schedule.”
Fiscal Fourth Quarter:
Net revenue for the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026 was $1.01 billion, with GAAP net loss of $7.2 billion, or $84.65 per diluted share. The GAAP net loss was driven by the equitization of certain amounts of our convertible notes in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026, which contributed to a one-time, non-cash loss on debt extinguishment of $7.8 billion. Net revenue for the third quarter of fiscal year 2026 was $808.4 million, with GAAP net income of $144.2 million, or $1.50 per diluted share. Net revenue for the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2025 was $480.7 million, with GAAP net income of $213.3 million, or $2.96 per diluted share.
Non-GAAP net income for the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026 was $326.3 million, or $3.23 per diluted share. Non-GAAP net income for the third quarter of fiscal year 2026 was $225.7 million, or $2.37 per diluted share. Non-GAAP net income for the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2025 was $63.3 million, or $0.88 per diluted share.
The Company held $2.7 billion in total cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments at the end of the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026, a decrease of $433.9 million from the end of the third quarter of fiscal year 2026.
Full Fiscal Year 2026:
Net revenue for fiscal year 2026 was $3.01 billion, with GAAP net loss of $6.9 billion, or $92.96 per diluted share. The GAAP net loss was driven by the equitization of certain amounts of our convertible notes in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026, which contributed to a one-time, non-cash loss on debt extinguishment of $7.8 billion. Net revenue for fiscal year 2025 was $1.6 billion, with GAAP net income of $25.9 million, or $0.37 per diluted share.
Non-GAAP net income for fiscal year 2026 was $782.3 million, or $8.67 per diluted share. Non-GAAP net income for fiscal year 2025 was $146.4 million, or $2.06 per diluted share.
The Company held $2.7 billion in total cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments at the end of the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026, an increase of $1.9 billion from the end of fiscal year 2025.

Lumentum (NASDAQ: LITE) is a global leader in optical and photonic technologies that power the networks and infrastructure behind AI, cloud computing, and next-generation communications. Built on decades of photonics innovation, Lumentum delivers high-performance lasers, modules, and optical subsystems that enable scalable, energy-efficient data center connectivity, advanced telecom networks, industrial manufacturing, and sensing applications. Headquartered in San Jose, California, the company operates R&D, manufacturing, and sales facilities worldwide. Learn more at www.lumentum.com.
